title: The age of revolutions
intro: From the American Revolution to the Congress of Vienna: French support for a rebellion, the monarchy it bankrupted, a revolution and its terror, an emperor who crowned himself, and the coalition that brought Europe back into balance.
end: A colony of 2.4 million won with a great power's money and fleet; the great power went bankrupt doing it; its revolution turned the nation into an army; a general turned the army into an empire and crowned himself; and Britain's credit and the coalitions it paid for restored a balance that lasted until 1914. steps.title: Thirteen colonies
steps.text: By 1775 the Thirteen Colonies had 2.4 million people. On 14 June 1775 Congress created the Continental Army from 22,000 troops outside Boston and 5,000 at New York City. About 250,000 Americans served, but never more than 90,000 at any one time.

steps.title: Saratoga
steps.text: At Saratoga, Burgoyne's army of 5,791 men faced about 12,000 colonial troops, and he surrendered it on 17 October 1777. By some estimates up to 90% of the arms the Americans used in the campaign came from France.

steps.title: The French alliance
steps.text: Vergennes persuaded Louis XVI to fund a front company that bought munitions for the Patriots and shipped them in neutral Dutch ships. In February 1778 France signed a Treaty of Alliance with the Americans. It spent 1.3 billion livres supporting them directly.

steps.title: The Chesapeake and Yorktown
steps.text: At the Chesapeake de Grasse had 24 ships of the line, Graves 19. At Yorktown about 19,000 Franco-American troops, with the 6,000 French soldiers Rochambeau had landed in 1780, besieged the British; 8,000 soldiers and 214 guns were captured. The Treaty of Paris was signed on 3 September 1783.

steps.title: The debt
steps.text: The American war cost France 1,066 million livres, paid with new loans at high interest and no new taxes, and raised its debt to about 3.3 billion livres. By 1788 half of the state's revenue went on servicing the debt. The Church held upwards of 7% of France's land and took 150 million livres a year.

steps.text: The Estates-General of 1789 had 1,219 deputies: 302 for the clergy, 289 for the nobility and 611 for the Third Estate, which stood for about 98% of some 28 million people. The clergy itself numbered 115,000 to 150,000.

steps.title: The Bastille
steps.text: On 14 July 1789 the Bastille, holding only seven inmates, was stormed. The Assembly abolished feudalism, put the Church under state control and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man. On 2 November 1789 the Church's property was nationalised and used to back the assignats.

steps.title: The king's execution
steps.text: On 21 January 1793 Louis XVI, aged 38, was guillotined on the Place de la Révolution. That year Austria, Sardinia, Naples, Prussia, Spain and Great Britain formed the First Coalition against revolutionary France. Marie Antoinette was executed on 16 October 1793.

steps.text: In February 1793 the Convention decreed a levy of about 300,000 men. The Committee of Public Safety was formed on 6 April, and in August the levée en masse drafted all men aged 18 to 25. Between 750,000 and 800,000 were conscripted.

steps.title: The Terror
steps.text: From June 1793 the Terror issued 16,594 official death sentences, 2,639 of them in Paris; after the Law of 22 Prairial another 1,366 people were executed in seven weeks. On 28 July 1794 Robespierre and 21 of his followers were sentenced to death without a hearing.

steps.title: The emperor crowns himself
steps.text: Under the Concordat of 1801 the Pope recognised Bonaparte's regime and the regime recognised Catholicism as the religion of the great majority. In 1804 a plebiscite confirmed a hereditary empire: 3.5 million yes, the count inflated by 300,000 to 500,000. On 2 December 1804, at Notre-Dame, with Pope Pius VII present, Napoleon crowned himself. Britain, Russia, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire refused to recognise the title.

steps.title: Trafalgar
steps.text: Britain declared war on France in May 1803 and repeatedly financed France's enemies. In April 1805 it formed the Third Coalition with Austria and Russia. After 1793 it raised its sailors from 15,000 to 133,000. At Trafalgar, Nelson's 27 ships of the line met 33 French and Spanish; 18 were captured or destroyed, and Britain lost none.

steps.title: Austerlitz and Jena
steps.text: At Austerlitz Napoleon had some 72,000 men and 157 guns against about 85,000 Allies, 70% of them Russian, with 318 guns. The Allies lost about 36,000 of 89,000, 38% of their force. On 14 October 1806 the Grande Armée decisively defeated the Prussians, about 130,000 with 20,000 Saxons, at Jena and Auerstedt.

steps.title: Europe out of balance
steps.text: The Berlin Decree of 21 November 1806 barred Britain's trade from Europe, hurting France and its allies too. In 1808 Napoleon's Army of Spain, 278,670 men, faced 80,000 raw Spanish troops. In 1812 he deployed 600,000 soldiers against Russia, whose army peaked at 904,000. Of 615,000, only 110,000 came back.

steps.title: The alliance against France
steps.text: From 1793 to 1814 Britain paid its allies £46,289,549 in subsidies, which paid for about 450,000 Austrian and Russian soldiers at their 1813 peak. At Leipzig about 560,000 soldiers fought and 133,000 fell. In 1815 about 250,000 Frenchmen faced about 850,000 allies; at Waterloo Napoleon's 74,500 met Wellington and 50,000 arriving Prussians. Four days later he abdicated.

steps.title: The Congress of Vienna
steps.text: From September 1814 to June 1815 the Congress of Vienna, chaired by Metternich, resized the five Great Powers, Austria, Britain, Russia, Prussia and France, so that they would balance each other and remain at peace. Britain's debt had reached £679 million. The Concert of Europe kept the balance until the First World War in 1914.
